questions.question: What is the magnitude of $2\underset{\sim}{u}+3\underset{\sim}{v}$?
questions.answer: $|2\mathbf u+3\mathbf v|^2=4|\mathbf u|^2+12\,\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v+9|\mathbf v|^2$. This depends on $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$, which are not given, so the magnitude cannot be determined (D).

questions.question: The polynomial $P(x)=x^3+5x^2+bx+c$ has a double root at $x=-1$. What are the values of $b$ and $c$?
What is the value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\left(4\cos^2x-5\right)dx$?
questions.answer: $4\cos^2x-5=2(1+\cos2x)-5=2\cos2x-3$. $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}(2\cos2x-3)dx=\Big[\sin2x-3x\Big]_0^{\pi/4}=1-\dfrac{3\pi}4$ (A).

questions.question: Which of the following is equivalent to $\left|\operatorname{proj}_{\underset{\sim}{v}}\underset{\sim}{u}\right|$?
questions.answer: $\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf v}\mathbf u=\dfrac{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v}{|\mathbf v|^2}\mathbf v$, so its magnitude is $\dfrac{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v|}{|\mathbf v|^2}|\mathbf v|=\dfrac{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v|}{|\mathbf v|}$ (C). The absolute value is needed since the magnitude is never negative (B can be negative).

questions.question: Which of the following gives the same curve as $x=\sin t$ and $y=-t$, for all real numbers $t$?
questions.answer: The original curve is $x=\sin(-y)=-\sin y$. A: $x=\sin y$, which is a different curve. C and D: $y=t^2+\pi$ or $y=-t^2$ cannot take all real values, so they give only part of the curve. B: $y=2t+\pi$ takes all real values and $x=-\sin(2t+\pi)=-\sin y$, which is the same curve (B).

questions.question: How many seven letter words can be formed from the word THUNDER, such that T and R must be at either end, and U is somewhere to the right of D?
questions.answer: T and R occupy the two ends in $2!=2$ ways. The other five letters fill the middle, and U is to the right of D in exactly half of the $5!$ arrangements, i.e. $\dfrac{5!}{2}=60$. Total $=2\times60=120$ (B).

questions.question: What is the number of solutions to the equation $x+e^{-x}=\big||x|-2\big|$?
questions.answer: Sketch $y=x+e^{-x}$ and $y=\big||x|-2\big|$ (a W shape with minima at $x=\pm2$ and a local maximum of 2 at $x=0$). For large positive $x$, $e^{-x}\to0$ so the exponential curve approaches $y=x$, which lies above the right arm $y=x-2$ and so never meets it. The curve $y=x+e^{-x}$ has a minimum value of 1 at $x=0$ and crosses the middle part of the W (the peak region near $x=0$) twice, once either side of the $y$-axis. There are no other intersections, so there are 2 solutions (C).

questions.question: The gradient of the normal at any point $P$ on a particular curve is half the gradient of the line joining $P$ and the origin. Which of the following differential equations does this curve satisfy?
questions.answer: Normal gradient $=-\dfrac1{dy/dx}$ and the gradient of $OP$ is $\dfrac yx$. So $-\dfrac1{dy/dx}=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac yx$. Taking reciprocals, $-\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{2x}y$, i.e. $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+\dfrac{2x}y=0$ (C).

questions.question: Let $f(x)=\sin(2x)-\sqrt3\cos(2x)$. What is the value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{f(x)}2\right)dx$?
questions.answer: $f(x)=2\sin\left(2x-\dfrac\pi3\right)$, so the integrand is $\sin^{-1}\left(\sin\left(2x-\dfrac\pi3\right)\right)$. Let $u=2x-\dfrac\pi3$, $du=2dx$; the limits become $-\dfrac\pi3$ to $\dfrac{2\pi}3$: $I=\dfrac12\displaystyle\int_{-\pi/3}^{2\pi/3}\sin^{-1}(\sin u)\,du$. The graph of $\sin^{-1}(\sin u)$ equals $u$ for $|u|\le\dfrac\pi2$ and $\pi-u$ for $\dfrac\pi2\le u\le\dfrac{3\pi}2$. The integral is the signed area: $\displaystyle\int_{-\pi/3}^{\pi/2}u\,du=\dfrac12\left(\dfrac{\pi^2}4-\dfrac{\pi^2}9\right)=\dfrac{5\pi^2}{72}$ and $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/2}^{2\pi/3}(\pi-u)du=\dfrac12\left(\dfrac\pi2\right)^2-\dfrac12\left(\dfrac\pi3\right)^2=\dfrac{5\pi^2}{72}$. Total $=\dfrac{5\pi^2}{36}$, so $I=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{5\pi^2}{36}=\dfrac{5\pi^2}{72}$ (D).

questions.question: Distinct factors of $337\,500$ are randomly selected. What is the minimum number of distinct factors of $337\,500$ that must be selected to guarantee that the product of these selected factors will be a multiple of $337\,500$?
questions.answer: $337\,500=2^2\times3^3\times5^5$. The product is a multiple of $337\,500$ only if the exponents of 2, 3 and 5 in the product sum to at least 2, 3 and 5 respectively. Worst case: select all factors with no factor of 2, i.e. $3^a5^b$ with $0\le a\le3$, $0\le b\le5$, which is $4\times6=24$ factors. Their product contains no 2. Adding one more factor (which must contain at least one 2, e.g. $2^1$) gives only $2^1$, still not enough (25 factors). A 26th factor adds at least another 2, so the power of 2 is at least $2^2$, and since all 24 factors without 2 are included, the powers of 3 and 5 are far more than needed. So 26 factors are needed (B). (Leaving out all factors with no 3 or no 5 gives smaller worst-case sets of 18 and 12 factors respectively.)

questions.question: Differentiate $(\tan^{-1}x)^2$.
questions.answer: $\dfrac d{dx}(\tan^{-1}x)^2=2\tan^{-1}x\cdot\dfrac1{1+x^2}=\dfrac{2\tan^{-1}x}{1+x^2}$.

questions.question: Use the substitution $u=x+2$ to find $\displaystyle\int(x-1)\sqrt{x+2}\,dx$.
questions.answer: $x=u-2$ and $du=dx$. $\displaystyle\int(u-3)u^{1/2}du=\int\left(u^{3/2}-3u^{1/2}\right)du=\dfrac25u^{5/2}-2u^{3/2}+C=\dfrac25(x+2)^{5/2}-2(x+2)^{3/2}+C$.

questions.question: Solve $\dfrac x{1-x^2}<0$.
questions.answer: Multiply both sides by $(1-x^2)^2>0$ (valid for $x\ne\pm1$): $x(1-x^2)<0$, i.e. $x(1-x)(1+x)<0$. The cubic has negative leading coefficient and zeroes at $-1,0,1$, so it is negative for $-1<x<0$ and $x>1$. These avoid $x=\pm1$ (undefined) and $x=0$ (equals 0). Solution: $-1<x<0$ or $x>1$.

questions.question: Consider the function $f(x)=\dfrac{x-2}{x-5}$. State the range of $f^{-1}(x)$.
questions.answer: The range of $f^{-1}$ is the domain of $f$: all real $x$ with $x\ne5$.

questions.question: Consider the function $f(x)=\dfrac{x-2}{x-5}$. Find an expression for $f^{-1}(x)$.
questions.answer: Swap $x$ and $y$: $x=\dfrac{y-2}{y-5}$. Then $xy-5x=y-2$, so $y(x-1)=5x-2$ and $f^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{5x-2}{x-1}$.

questions.question: The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown. It has a maximum at $(-1,1)$, $x$-intercepts at $-3$ and $1$, and $y$-intercept $\tfrac23$. Sketch the graph of $y=\dfrac1{f(x)}$, clearly showing all important features.
questions.answer: Features: vertical asymptotes at $x=-3$ and $x=1$ (the zeroes of $f$); horizontal asymptote $y=0$ (as $f\to\pm\infty$); $y$-intercept $\dfrac32$; a minimum at $(-1,1)$ between the asymptotes (the reciprocal of the maximum of $f$). The graph is above the $x$-axis for $-3<x<1$ and below it outside this interval, passing through the points where $f=-1$ (the same points as $f$). Sketch:

questions.question: The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown. It has a maximum at $(-1,1)$, $x$-intercepts at $-3$ and $1$, and $y$-intercept $\tfrac23$. Sketch the graph of $y^2=|f(x)|$, clearly showing all important features.
questions.answer: First sketch $y=|f(x)|$ (reflect the part below the $x$-axis upwards), then $y=\pm\sqrt{|f(x)|}$. Features: $x$-intercepts at $-3$ and $1$ (with vertical tangents there); symmetric about the $x$-axis; $y$-intercepts $\pm\sqrt{\tfrac23}$; the points $(-1,\pm1)$; between $-3$ and $1$ the curve is outside the graph of $y=f(x)$ since $\sqrt{|f|}>|f|$ when $|f|<1$ (so it lies above $f$ there); outside this interval the curves $y=\pm\sqrt{-f(x)}$ continue to grow like $\pm\sqrt{|x|}$. questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int3\cos(2x)\cos\left(5x-\dfrac\pi3\right)dx$.
questions.answer: Using $\cos A\cos B=\dfrac12[\cos(A-B)+\cos(A+B)]$ with $A=2x$, $B=5x-\dfrac\pi3$: $\cos2x\cos\left(5x-\dfrac\pi3\right)=\dfrac12\left[\cos\left(3x-\dfrac\pi3\right)+\cos\left(7x-\dfrac\pi3\right)\right]$ (cosine is even). So $\displaystyle\int=\dfrac32\left[\dfrac13\sin\left(3x-\dfrac\pi3\right)+\dfrac17\sin\left(7x-\dfrac\pi3\right)\right]+C=\dfrac12\sin\left(3x-\dfrac\pi3\right)+\dfrac3{14}\sin\left(7x-\dfrac\pi3\right)+C$.

questions.question: Solve $2\operatorname{cosec}\theta-4\cot\theta=3$ using the $t$-formula, for $0\le\theta\le2\pi$. Give your answer(s) correct to 3 significant figures.
questions.answer: Let $t=\tan\dfrac\theta2$: $\sin\theta=\dfrac{2t}{1+t^2}$ and $\tan\theta=\dfrac{2t}{1-t^2}$, so $\operatorname{cosec}\theta=\dfrac{1+t^2}{2t}$ and $\cot\theta=\dfrac{1-t^2}{2t}$. Then $\dfrac{2(1+t^2)-4(1-t^2)}{2t}=3$, so $6t^2-2=6t$, i.e. $3t^2-3t-1=0$ and $t=\dfrac{3\pm\sqrt{21}}6$. $\dfrac\theta2=\arctan\dfrac{3+\sqrt{21}}6$ gives $\theta=1.80$; $\dfrac\theta2=\pi+\arctan\dfrac{3-\sqrt{21}}6$ (the principal value is negative, so add $\pi$) gives $\theta=5.77$. Both lie in $[0,2\pi]$. Also $\theta=\pi$ ($t$ undefined) is not a solution since $\cot\pi$ is undefined. $\theta=1.80,\ 5.77$.

questions.question: The region enclosed by $y=e^{-x}$, $y=x$, $x=1$ and $x=3$ is rotated about the $x$-axis. Calculate the volume of the solid of revolution. Give your answer in fully simplified exact form.
questions.answer: On $[1,3]$, $x\ge1>e^{-x}$, so $y=x$ is on top. $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_1^3\left(x^2-e^{-2x}\right)dx=\pi\left[\dfrac{x^3}3+\dfrac12e^{-2x}\right]_1^3=\pi\left[\left(9+\dfrac12e^{-6}\right)-\left(\dfrac13+\dfrac12e^{-2}\right)\right]=\pi\left(\dfrac{26}3+\dfrac12e^{-6}-\dfrac12e^{-2}\right)$ cubic units.

questions.question: Let $\underset{\sim}{u}=2\mathbf i+5\mathbf j$ and $\underset{\sim}{v}=-3\mathbf i+\lambda^2\mathbf j$, where $\lambda$ is a real number. Determine the values of $\lambda$ such that $\underset{\sim}{u}$ and $\underset{\sim}{v}$ are perpendicular.
questions.answer: $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=-6+5\lambda^2=0$, so $\lambda^2=\dfrac65$ and $\lambda=\pm\sqrt{\dfrac65}$.

questions.question: Let $\underset{\sim}{u}=2\mathbf i+5\mathbf j$ and $\underset{\sim}{v}=-3\mathbf i+\lambda^2\mathbf j$, where $\lambda$ is a real number. Explain why $\underset{\sim}{u}$ cannot be parallel to $\underset{\sim}{v}$. (Justify your answer mathematically.)
questions.answer: If parallel, there is a real $r$ with $\mathbf u=r\mathbf v$: $2=-3r$ and $5=r\lambda^2$. The first gives $r=-\dfrac23$, so $\lambda^2=5\div\left(-\dfrac23\right)=-7.5$, which is impossible for real $\lambda$. Hence $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ are never parallel. (Alternatively, $\mathbf u$ points into the first quadrant while $\mathbf v$ has negative $x$-component and non-negative $y$-component, so they cannot be scalar multiples.)

questions.question: Let $\underset{\sim}{u}=2\mathbf i+5\mathbf j$ and $\underset{\sim}{v}=-3\mathbf i+\lambda^2\mathbf j$. If $\lambda=1$, determine $\underset{\sim}{q}$ such that $\underset{\sim}{u}=\operatorname{proj}_{\underset{\sim}{v}}(\underset{\sim}{u})+\underset{\sim}{q}$.
questions.answer: With $\lambda=1$, $\mathbf v=(-3,1)$. $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=-6+5=-1$ and $\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf v=10$. $\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf v}\mathbf u=\dfrac{-1}{10}(-3,1)=(0.3,-0.1)$. $\mathbf q=\mathbf u-\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf v}\mathbf u=(2-0.3,\ 5+0.1)=\begin{pmatrix}1.7\\5.1\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.question: The roots of $P(x)=8x^3-5x^2+2x-1$ are $\alpha,\beta$ and $\gamma$. Find the value of $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$.
questions.answer: $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=\dfrac58$ and $\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma=\dfrac28=\dfrac14$. $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2-2(\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma)=\dfrac{25}{64}-\dfrac12=-\dfrac7{64}$. (This is negative, so $P$ has non-real roots.)

questions.question: The triangle $ABC$ is right angled at $A$. Let $AB=5$ cm and $\angle ABC=\theta$ radians. If $\theta$ is increasing at a constant rate of $0.1$ radians per second, find the rate at which the perimeter of the triangle is increasing when $\theta=\dfrac\pi3$ radians. Leave your answer in exact form.
questions.answer: $AC=5\tan\theta$ and $BC=\dfrac5{\cos\theta}=5\sec\theta$. Perimeter $p=5+5\tan\theta+5\sec\theta$. $\dfrac{dp}{d\theta}=5\sec^2\theta+5\sec\theta\tan\theta$. $\dfrac{dp}{dt}=\dfrac{dp}{d\theta}\cdot\dfrac{d\theta}{dt}=0.1\left(5\sec^2\theta+5\sec\theta\tan\theta\right)$. At $\theta=\dfrac\pi3$: $\sec=2$, $\tan=\sqrt3$, so $\dfrac{dp}{dt}=0.1(20+10\sqrt3)=2+\sqrt3$ cm/s.

questions.question: Prove by mathematical induction that, for all integers $n\ge1$, $2\times1!+5\times2!+10\times3!+\cdots+(n^2+1)\times n!=n\times(n+1)!$.
questions.answer:
$n=1$: LHS $=(1+1)\times1!=2$, RHS $=1\times2!=2$. True.

Assume true for $n=k$: $2\times1!+\cdots+(k^2+1)k!=k(k+1)!$.

For $n=k+1$: LHS $=k(k+1)!+\left[(k+1)^2+1\right](k+1)!=(k+1)!\left[k+k^2+2k+2\right]=(k+1)!\left(k^2+3k+2\right)=(k+1)!(k+1)(k+2)=(k+1)(k+2)!$, which is RHS for $n=k+1$. By induction it is true for all $n\ge1$.

questions.question: Show that $\dfrac1{2000}\left(\dfrac1S+\dfrac1{2000-S}\right)=\dfrac1{S(2000-S)}$.

The rate of spread of a flu is modelled by $\dfrac{dS}{dt}=\dfrac{S(2000-S)}{5000}$, where $S$ is the total number of people infected after $t$ days. Solve the differential equation using separation of variables to show that $S=\dfrac{2000}{1+Qe^{-0.4t}}$, where $Q$ is a constant.
questions.answer: $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dS}{S(2000-S)}=\int\dfrac{dt}{5000}$. By part (i), $\dfrac1{2000}\int\left(\dfrac1S+\dfrac1{2000-S}\right)dS=\dfrac t{5000}+C$, so $\ln\left|\dfrac S{2000-S}\right|=0.4t+C_1$ (multiplying by 2000). Hence $\dfrac S{2000-S}=Ae^{0.4t}$ ($A=\pm e^{C_1}$). $S=Ae^{0.4t}(2000-S)$, so $S\left(1+Ae^{0.4t}\right)=2000Ae^{0.4t}$ and $S=\dfrac{2000Ae^{0.4t}}{1+Ae^{0.4t}}=\dfrac{2000}{1+\frac1Ae^{-0.4t}}$. With $Q=\dfrac1A$: $S=\dfrac{2000}{1+Qe^{-0.4t}}$.

questions.question: The slope field of $\dfrac{dS}{dt}=\dfrac{S(2000-S)}{5000}$ is shown, with three regions labelled A (above $S=2000$), B (between $S=0$ and $S=2000$) and C (below $S=0$). Consider the particular solution $S=\dfrac{2000}{1+199e^{-0.4t}}$. In which one of these three regions will the curve of the particular solution lie? You must justify your answer.
questions.answer: For $t\ge0$, $199e^{-0.4t}>0$, so $1+199e^{-0.4t}>1$ and $0<S<2000$. At $t=0$, $S=\dfrac{2000}{200}=10$ and as $t\to\infty$, $S\to2000$ from below. So the curve lies entirely in region B.

questions.question: According to this model, and using $Q=199$, after how many days does the rate of spread reach its maximum? Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
questions.answer: $\dfrac{dS}{dt}=\dfrac{S(2000-S)}{5000}$ is a downward parabola in $S$ with its maximum at $S=1000$. Set $\dfrac{2000}{1+199e^{-0.4t}}=1000$: $1+199e^{-0.4t}=2$, so $e^{-0.4t}=\dfrac1{199}$ and $t=\dfrac{\ln199}{0.4}=13.23$ days.

questions.question: In $\triangle ABC$, $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of $AB$ and $AC$ respectively. Let $\overrightarrow{AB}=\underset{\sim}{b}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}=\underset{\sim}{c}$. Show that $\overrightarrow{BN}=\dfrac12\underset{\sim}{c}-\underset{\sim}{b}$, and write a similar expression for $\overrightarrow{CM}$.
questions.answer: $\overrightarrow{BN}=\overrightarrow{BA}+\overrightarrow{AN}=-\mathbf b+\dfrac12\mathbf c=\dfrac12\mathbf c-\mathbf b$. $\overrightarrow{CM}=\overrightarrow{CA}+\overrightarrow{AM}=-\mathbf c+\dfrac12\mathbf b=\dfrac12\mathbf b-\mathbf c$.

questions.question: In $\triangle ABC$, $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of $AB$ and $AC$ respectively. Let $\overrightarrow{AB}=\underset{\sim}{b}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}=\underset{\sim}{c}$. Hence, using vectors, show that if $BN$ and $CM$ are perpendicular, then $|\mathbf b|^2+|\mathbf c|^2=5|\mathbf a|^2$, where $\mathbf a=\overrightarrow{BC}$.
questions.answer: Perpendicular: $\overrightarrow{BN}\cdot\overrightarrow{CM}=0$. $\left(\dfrac12\mathbf c-\mathbf b\right)\cdot\left(\dfrac12\mathbf b-\mathbf c\right)=\dfrac14\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c-\dfrac12|\mathbf c|^2-\dfrac12|\mathbf b|^2+\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c=\dfrac54\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c-\dfrac12\left(|\mathbf b|^2+|\mathbf c|^2\right)=0$, so $\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c=\dfrac25\left(|\mathbf b|^2+|\mathbf c|^2\right)$ (1). Now $\mathbf a=\overrightarrow{BC}=\mathbf c-\mathbf b$, so $|\mathbf a|^2=|\mathbf b|^2+|\mathbf c|^2-2\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c$. Substituting (1): $|\mathbf a|^2=\left(|\mathbf b|^2+|\mathbf c|^2\right)\left(1-\dfrac45\right)=\dfrac15\left(|\mathbf b|^2+|\mathbf c|^2\right)$. Hence $|\mathbf b|^2+|\mathbf c|^2=5|\mathbf a|^2$.

questions.question: The position vectors of particles $P$ and $Q$ at time $t$ minutes are $\begin{pmatrix}\cos t\\\sin t\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}\cos3t\\\sin3t\end{pmatrix}$ respectively, where $0\le t\le2\pi$. Let $\theta$ be the angle between the vectors $\overrightarrow{OP}$ and $\overrightarrow{OQ}$ at time $t$, where $O$ is the origin. Show that $\cos\theta=\cos2t$.
questions.answer: $|\overrightarrow{OP}|=|\overrightarrow{OQ}|=1$, so $\cos\theta=\overrightarrow{OP}\cdot\overrightarrow{OQ}=\cos t\cos3t+\sin t\sin3t=\cos(3t-t)=\cos2t$.

questions.question: The position vectors of particles $P$ and $Q$ at time $t$ minutes are $\begin{pmatrix}\cos t\\\sin t\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}\cos3t\\\sin3t\end{pmatrix}$ respectively, where $0\le t\le2\pi$. Let $\theta$ be the angle between the vectors $\overrightarrow{OP}$ and $\overrightarrow{OQ}$ at time $t$, where $O$ is the origin. Find the total time for which $\theta\ge\dfrac\pi4$.
questions.answer: $0\le\theta\le\pi$ and $\cos$ is decreasing on this interval, so $\theta\ge\dfrac\pi4\iff\cos\theta\le\dfrac1{\sqrt2}\iff\cos2t\le\dfrac1{\sqrt2}$. For $0\le2t\le4\pi$ this holds for $2t\in\left[\dfrac\pi4,\dfrac{7\pi}4\right]\cup\left[\dfrac{9\pi}4,\dfrac{15\pi}4\right]$, i.e. $t\in\left[\dfrac\pi8,\dfrac{7\pi}8\right]\cup\left[\dfrac{9\pi}8,\dfrac{15\pi}8\right]$. Each interval has length $\dfrac{3\pi}4$, so the total time is $\dfrac{3\pi}2$ minutes.

questions.question: A particle is projected from the origin $O$ with initial speed $U$ and angle of elevation $\alpha$, where $0<\alpha<\dfrac\pi2$. The position vector at time $t$ after projection, where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity, is $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=\begin{pmatrix}Ut\cos\alpha\\Ut\sin\alpha-\dfrac{gt^2}2\end{pmatrix}$. (Do NOT prove this.) Prove that if the particle passes through the point $P(a,b)$, where $a>0$, then the minimum possible value of $U$ is $\sqrt{g\left(b+\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\right)}$.
questions.answer:
Eliminate $t=\dfrac x{U\cos\alpha}$: $y=x\tan\alpha-\dfrac{gx^2}{2U^2}\sec^2\alpha=x\tan\alpha-\dfrac{gx^2}{2U^2}\left(1+\tan^2\alpha\right)$. Passing through $(a,b)$ with $T=\tan\alpha$: $b=aT-\dfrac{ga^2}{2U^2}(1+T^2)$, so $\dfrac{ga^2}{2U^2}T^2-aT+\left(b+\dfrac{ga^2}{2U^2}\right)=0$.

For a real $\alpha$ to exist the discriminant must be non-negative: $a^2-4\cdot\dfrac{ga^2}{2U^2}\left(b+\dfrac{ga^2}{2U^2}\right)\ge0$. Dividing by $a^2$: $1\ge\dfrac{2g}{U^2}\left(b+\dfrac{ga^2}{2U^2}\right)$, so $U^2\ge2gb+\dfrac{g^2a^2}{U^2}$, i.e. $U^4-2gbU^2-g^2a^2\ge0$. Complete the square: $(U^2-gb)^2\ge g^2b^2+g^2a^2$, so $|U^2-gb|\ge g\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$. Since $U^2-gb\le-g\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ would give $U^2\le g(b-\sqrt{a^2+b^2})\le0$, which is impossible, we need $U^2\ge g\left(b+\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\right)$. The minimum possible value of $U$ is $\sqrt{g\left(b+\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\right)}$.

questions.question: A particle is projected from the origin $O$ with initial speed $U$ and angle of elevation $\alpha$, where $0<\alpha<\dfrac\pi2$. The position vector at time $t$ after projection, where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity, is $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=\begin{pmatrix}Ut\cos\alpha\\Ut\sin\alpha-\dfrac{gt^2}2\end{pmatrix}$. (Do NOT prove this.) Suppose the particle is projected with the minimum possible speed in order to pass through $P(a,b)$. Show that $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{b+\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}a$.
questions.answer: At the minimum speed the discriminant is zero, so the quadratic $\dfrac{ga^2}{2U^2}T^2-aT+\left(b+\dfrac{ga^2}{2U^2}\right)=0$ has the repeated root $T=\dfrac{a}{2\cdot\frac{ga^2}{2U^2}}=\dfrac{U^2}{ga}$. With $U^2=g\left(b+\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\right)$: $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{b+\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}a$.

questions.question: A particle is projected from the origin $O$ with initial speed $U$ and angle of elevation $\alpha$, where $0<\alpha<\dfrac\pi2$. The position vector at time $t$ after projection, where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity, is $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=\begin{pmatrix}Ut\cos\alpha\\Ut\sin\alpha-\dfrac{gt^2}2\end{pmatrix}$. (Do NOT prove this.) The particle is projected with the minimum possible speed to pass through $P(a,b)$. Deduce that $\underset{\sim}{v}(0)$ bisects the angle between $OP$ and the positive $y$-axis, where $\underset{\sim}{v}(0)$ is the initial velocity vector of the particle.
questions.answer:
Let $\beta$ be the angle $OP$ makes with the positive $x$-axis, so $\tan\beta=\dfrac ba$. The initial velocity makes angle $\alpha$ with the $x$-axis. The angle between $\mathbf v(0)$ and the positive $y$-axis is $\dfrac\pi2-\alpha$ and the angle between $OP$ and $\mathbf v(0)$ is $\alpha-\beta$. To show: $\dfrac\pi2-\alpha=\alpha-\beta$ (this requires $\alpha>\beta$, which holds since $\tan\alpha>\dfrac ba$).

$\tan\left(\dfrac\pi2-\alpha\right)=\cot\alpha=\dfrac a{b+\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}$. Let $r=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$. $\tan(\alpha-\beta)=\dfrac{\tan\alpha-\tan\beta}{1+\tan\alpha\tan\beta}=\dfrac{\frac{b+r}a-\frac ba}{1+\frac{b(b+r)}{a^2}}=\dfrac{r/a}{\frac{a^2+b^2+br}{a^2}}=\dfrac{ar}{r^2+br}=\dfrac a{r+b}$. The two tangents are equal and both angles lie in $\left(0,\dfrac\pi2\right)$, so $\dfrac\pi2-\alpha=\alpha-\beta$: $\mathbf v(0)$ bisects the angle between $OP$ and the positive $y$-axis.
